stances.claim: Aquino v. Aquino is a courageous corrective: by adopting 'nonmarital' for children born outside wedlock and recognizing their right to inherit from grandparents by representation, the Court partly shatters the Article 992 'iron curtain' without overstepping into judicial legislation.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal-reform endorsement bounded by separation-of-powers respect

stances.claim: Children born outside wedlock are innocent -- 'illegitimate parents,' not 'illegitimate children' -- a sentiment CJ has held since law school under Prof. Edgardo L. Paras, who urged him to 'amend the law' himself.

The historical disability layered from the Spanish Civil Code through the 1950 Civil Code (natural / natural-by-legal-fiction / spurious) to the Family Code's binary (legitimate / illegitimate) bred 'antagonism, hate, and bitterness' -- the iron curtain's social cost is real.
stances.rhetorical_move: historical-injury narrative as warrant for reform

stances.claim: The Court properly grounded its reform on 1987 Constitution policies and international treaties protecting child welfare -- and rightly refused to be 'duty bound to uncritically parrot archaic prejudices and cruelties.' The best interest of the child should prevail.

notable_anecdotes: Christmas-week framing: the Holy Child 'strictly speaking, was conceived and born in the laylayan and outside a human marriage' -- using the season's iconography to dignify nonmarital birth.

Law-school exchange with Prof. Edgardo L. Paras: CJ saying 'Sir, I believe that in reality, and in fact, there are no illegitimate children, only illegitimate parents,' and Paras replying with a smile, 'I agree. So, please aspire to be a future legislator and amend the law.'
Court's editorial discipline: carefully avoiding 'illegitimate' across 47 pages while quoting the statute it could not amend.

one_paragraph_summary: On the day after Christmas, Panganiban turns to the Supreme Court's care for 'the least, the last, and the lost' -- the 'laylayan ng lipunan' -- by featuring Aquino v. Aquino (Dec. 7, 2021), the 47-page ponencia of Senior Associate Justice Marvic M.V.F. Leonen. The decision reverses traditional norms in two ways. First, lexical: the Court refuses to use the 'pejorative and disparaging' label 'illegitimate' for children born of parents not married to each other and coins 'nonmarital' instead -- explaining that, beyond children born to parents with marriage impediments, nonmarital birth covers parents below marriageable age, victims of sexual assault who refused to marry the perpetrator, fathers who died before birth, and parents who chose not to marry though qualified. The Court cannot amend the statute, only interpret it. Second, substantive: it recognizes the right of such children to inherit 'by representation' from their grandparents who died intestate, partly shattering the 'iron curtain' of Article 992 of the Civil Code, which had barred inheritance ab intestato between legitimate and illegitimate lines. Panganiban traces the historical layering of the disability: from the Spanish conquistadores' Civil Code in 'this blessed land of the morning,' through the 1950 Civil Code's trichotomy (natural, natural by legal fiction, spurious), to the 1988 Family Code's legitimate/illegitimate binary that nonetheless preserved many earlier disabilities. He shares his own law-school exchange with Prof. Edgardo L. Paras (later a Supreme Court justice): 'there are no illegitimate children, only illegitimate parents.' The Court -- anchored on 1987 Constitution policies and international treaties -- courageously held that 'we are not duty bound to uncritically parrot archaic prejudices and cruelties' and that 'the best interest of the child should prevail.' He notes in passing SAJ Leonen's parallel Writ of Kalayaan project, worth another column.
